summary:
Kerala stands under India's national transgender-rights framework while operating a substantial state layer of its own. In November 2015 it adopted the country's first government transgender policy, addressing the right to identify as "male", "female" or "TG" (third gender) and providing for equal access to social and economic resources, equal treatment under law, life, liberty and justice, and non-discrimination on grounds of sex.

Kerala is among the states and union territories reported to Parliament in December 2021 as having constituted a Transgender Welfare Board under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules, the body that coordinates state benefits for transgender residents.

Surgical care has been a state project with persistent delivery gaps. In March 2016 the Social Justice Department proposed free sex reassignment surgery in government hospitals, at least in medical colleges, from the next financial year. Before that proposal there was no in-state SRS facility, and patients travelled to Chennai or Bengaluru at costs of Rs 2–5 lakh for male-to-female and Rs 4–8 lakh for female-to-male procedures, on top of six months to two years of counselling, a year or more of hormone therapy and post-surgery observation. Implementation depended on health ministry approval and on training multidisciplinary teams in urology, endocrinology, sexology and psychology. Many government hospitals still cannot offer surgery for want of trained staff, so patients fall back on costlier private institutions where care standards are uneven and where reimbursement schemes require patients to raise the full fee before any refund.

Two facilities mark the state's provision. The Government Medical College Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram completed its first sex reassignment surgery in January 2017 through staged procedures over three years. The Government Medical College Hospital in Kottayam opened in February 2017 what is described as the country's first government clinic exclusively for the transgender community, running twice a month with a specialised panel and also serving sex workers, after a District Legal Services Authority proposal prompted by transgender patients' reported apprehension about approaching hospitals and consequent reliance on self-medication. Health cards denoting transgender status were distributed through the clinic, and the same authority proposed separate public toilets for transgender persons to the district collector.

Deaths have driven policy. The suicide of Anannyah Kumari Alex, who alleged botched gender affirmation surgery, triggered protests over irregularities and the absence of a specific protocol in private hospitals; the state appointed an expert committee on transgender health-sector issues and initiated steps for free surgeries in government hospitals. The suicide of Praveen Nath, Kerala's first transgender bodybuilder, drew attention to transphobic groups described by Social Justice Minister R. Bindu as rooted in religious fundamentalism, with cyberbullying and transphobic media coverage identified as causes.

A recent spate of killings of transgender people, with lack of responsible police investigation, has raised security concerns, alongside a rise in police harassment when transgender people attend stations to file complaints. The Director General of Police issued a direction that such grievances be addressed without delay.

Recorded case numbers are very small and reflect police registration rather than incidence. Kerala accounted for 2 of the 7 nationwide Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 and 4 of the 11 in 2023, a joint-highest state total with Tamil Nadu in 2023. The reporting organisation cautions that national counts are tiny because of registration bias, so these figures understate violence.

Conversion therapy is widely practised by licensed psychiatrists and psychologists as well as by unqualified practitioners, despite position statements from multiple professional bodies condemning the practice as unscientific and illegal.

Public hostility is documented and has reached the courts. In December 2023 the High Court of Kerala described cyber attacks against the LGBT+ community as a "serious issue" and asked authorities to take necessary action. The October 2023 annual pride march in Malappuram was attacked by a homophobic mob, followed by a police lathicharge. At least two LGBTQ people have died by suicide amid what sources describe as all-time-high cyberbullying, and hate-speech allegations have been made against mainstream politicians. Opposition is attributed to meninist groups, conservative political groups, religious organisations and social conservatism.

Discrimination in employment and housing persists despite the state's early policy lead. Community resources include Queerythm's 24/7 helpline for members in distress, Queerala's campaigning on healthcare, curriculum and workplace policies, and Sahayathrika for LGBTIQA+ members assigned female at birth. The Kerala Queer Pride march in Thrissur has run since July 2010 and Queerythm walks since 2017, both focused on sensitising police and media to prevent violence and discrimination.
tangentialFactors:
Kerala's record is one of early policy leadership followed by incomplete implementation: it was the first state to adopt a transgender policy in 2015 and opened what is described as the country's first government transgender clinic in 2017, yet the same sources document absent surgical capacity, uneven private care standards, refund arrangements that require patients to pre-fund treatment, and discrimination in employment and housing as continuing major problems.

The state's high ranking on recorded Transgender Persons Act cases is a raw-count ranking with a national denominator of only 7 cases in 2021 and 11 in 2023, and the source itself attributes the small totals to police-registration bias. A joint-highest sub-national total on such a small base cannot be read as a measure of comparative danger, and no per-capita figure is provided.

Assessments of the social climate diverge in tone rather than in fact: sources describe an easing from prior invisibility, when few people came out for fear their family would "take them to a psychiatrist or file a police complaint against friends", alongside documented increases in cyberbullying, transphobic groups and organised opposition. Both trends are sourced to the same period.

The state's own institutions carry much of the protection machinery: a Transgender Welfare Board, a Social Justice Department that has convened workshops on identity cards, pensions and training, a state police direction on complaint handling, and a High Court that has intervened on cyber attacks against the community.
localsOnly:
The Transgender Welfare Board coordinates resident-facing benefits, and a 2017 Social Justice Department workshop in Kozhikode with around 30 transgender representatives covered identity cards, pension for those over 60, skill development training, scholarships, educational loans and driving lessons for employment. Kannur district allocated budget for employment and skill training, and the government later provided reimbursement for gender affirming surgeries plus scholarships for transgender students in classes 7 to 10.

Education and employment schemes have a mixed record. Kochi's first transgender school, opened in 2016 for 10th and 12th board exams and vocational training for 10 students aged 25 to 50, ceased functioning as a school after three months and became a hostel for transgender Kochi Metro staff. A transgender-owned and operated G Taxi equality-taxi service, open to all passengers, was set up to provide livelihood and public visibility. A Gender Park dedicated to gender equality and LGBT issues opened in Kozhikode in February 2016.

The state's own estimate put the transgender population at around 25,000, with about 81% wishing to transition and 76% concealing their identity for fear of non-acceptance.

Residents face employment and housing discrimination as the principal documented barriers, and the government clinic at Kottayam also serves sex workers, a group that had campaigned on health concerns before the District Legal Services Authority proposal.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the March 2016 proposal for free sex reassignment surgery in government hospitals was implemented statewide, and on what terms, is not resolved by these sources; they record the proposal, the training requirement and later steps following the Anannyah Kumari Alex protests, but no completion date or current coverage list.

No region-specific signal was identified on entry, visa or border-document screening for visitors, or on any differential screening of gender-nonconforming travellers at Kerala's airports or ports. The sources address residents and state services, not inbound travellers.

The crime figures are raw counts on a national base of 7 and 11 cases, with no per-capita denominator and an explicit registration-bias caveat; they cannot support a comparative risk ranking between states.

No Kerala-specific judicial ban on conversion therapy is sourced here, and the sources do not record enforcement action against practitioners despite professional bodies' position statements. Whether the 2015 policy's non-discrimination provisions have been enforced in any individual case is also not sourced.

The national layer, including the March 2026 amendment to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) framework, national passport and document rules, and other states' laws and incidents, is carried by the parent record and is not restated here.
